plain_english: Don't make your training about doing unnatural things just to impress people. If you do that, you're no different from street performers — even though you call yourself a philosopher. Sure, walking on a tightrope is hard. It's also dangerous. But does that mean we should practice tightrope walking? Or climbing palm trees? Or hugging statues? Of course not. Just because something is difficult and dangerous doesn't make it good practice. The only practice worth doing is what helps you achieve your actual goal.
original_excerpt: We ought not to make our exercises consist in means contrary to nature and adapted to cause admiration, for if we do so, we who call ourselves philosophers, shall not differ at all from jugglers. For it is difficult even to walk on a rope; and not only difficult, but it is also dangerous. Ought we for this reason to practice walking on a rope, or setting up a palm-tree, or embracing statues? By no means. Every thing which is difficult and dangerous is not suitable for practice; but that is suitable which conduces to the working out of that which is proposed to us.

plain_english: What's the goal we're working toward? To live with our desires and fears under control. What does that mean? It means you don't get disappointed when you want something, and you don't end up dealing with things you're trying to avoid. This is what all your practice should aim for. You can't master your desires and fears without serious, constant work. Here's the key: if you let yourself want and fear things that aren't under your control, you'll fail. You won't get what you want, and you won't avoid what you fear.
original_excerpt: And what is that which is proposed to us as a thing to be worked out? To live with desire and aversion (avoidance of certain things) free from restraint. And what is this? Neither to be disappointed in that which you desire, nor to fall into anything which you would avoid. Towards this object then exercise (practice) ought to tend. For since it is not possible to have your desire not disappointed and your aversion free from falling into that which you would avoid, without great and constant practice, you must know that if you allow your desire and aversion to turn to things which are not within the power of the will, you will neither have your desire capable of attaining your object, nor your aversion free from the power of avoiding that which you would avoid.

plain_english: We have strong habits. We're used to wanting and avoiding things that are out of our control. We need to build opposite habits to fight this. When something looks really tempting, that's when you need to practice your training the most. Eventually, when you're ready, you can test yourself at the right moment. You'll go into the arena to see if appearances still overpower you like they used to. But at first, stay far away from what's stronger than you. It's not a fair fight between a beautiful young woman and someone just starting philosophy. As they say, the clay pot and the rock don't mix well.
original_excerpt: And since strong habit leads (prevails), and we are accustomed to employ desire and aversion only to things which are not within the power of our will, we ought to oppose to this habit a contrary habit, and where there is great slipperiness in the appearances, there to oppose the habit of exercise. Then at last, if occasion presents itself, for the purpose of trying yourself at a proper time you will descend into the arena to know if appearances overpower you as they did formerly. But at first fly far from that which is stronger than yourself; the contest is unequal between a charming young girl and a beginner in philosophy. The earthen pitcher, as the saying is, and the rock do not agree.
